extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic and philosophy (advanced undergraduates/graduate-level readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and rules for forming, interpreting, manipulating, and inferring with disjunctive propositions and related indirect (contrapositive) methods of inference in formal logic. Includes symbolic laws, combination/distribution rules, and worked examples illustrating correct and incorrect inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive vs. non-exclusive alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether alternatives in a disjunctive proposition are intended to be exclusive or possibly true together (compossible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that alternatives are often exclusive in many contexts and that exclusive alternatives give more precision and clearness; older logicians directed that 'the Membra dividendi... should be exclusive of each other.' But many ordinary uses treat alternatives as compossible (both true at the same time) — Whately's example 'Virtue tends to procure us either the esteem of mankind, or the favour of God' (both may be true). Mill and others warn against always interpreting 'or' as exclusive (examples: knave or fool; saint or philosopher). Context (the matter, not the form) decides exclusivity; legal/bill wording can make non-exclusivity explicit (using 'or' in a particular form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select exclusive alternatives when possible for precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer exclusive divisions (mutually exclusive alternatives) when the subject permits, because they give greater precision and clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Old works on logic contained a rule directing that parts of a division 'should be exclusive of each other.' Use exclusive alternatives when the subject demands it (e.g., certain legal documents); but avoid forcing exclusivity where natural language or the matter does not support it (Mill's objection to universal exclusivity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Commutativeness for disjunction
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of alternatives in a disjunctive aggregate has no effect on meaning: A + B = B + A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'rich or rare gems' as identical to 'rare or rich gems.' Symbolically expressed (A + B = B + A). This law holds for any aggregate of alternatives and underlies that disjunctive terms are commutative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Unity (A + A = A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any number of identical alternatives in a disjunction reduce to a single alternative; A + A = A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If P is asserted to be Q or R and later Q is shown to be another name for R, the disjunction reduces to the single alternative. This law distinguishes logical terms from mathematical terms (does not apply to numerical units) and is analogous to the Law of Simplicity (AA = A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between combined and disjunctive terms (De Morgan-like)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every disjunctive term is the negative of a corresponding combined term, and reciprocally the negative of a combined term is a disjunction of negatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Negative of 'malleable-dense-metal' is 'not-malleable or not-dense or not-metallic.' This follows from the idea that the negative of a conjunction is the disjunction of the negatives; interpret 'or' here as unexclusive (objects may be not-malleable and not-dense simultaneously). This explains why writing negatives of combined terms by exclusive 'or' would require enumerating many alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic Law of Duality (A = AB .|. Ab)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every term A either agrees with B or does not agree with B; expressed symbolically as A = AB .|. Ab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formula is asserted to be fundamental and to lie at the basis of reasoning. The law is repeatedly employed in substitution and inference processes (basis for indirect methods). The author emphasizes why A must appear in both alternatives (to ensure every term has a negative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recapitulation of fundamental Laws of Thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The three fundamental Laws of Thought in symbolic form: Law of Identity (A = A), Law of Contradiction, Law of Duality (A = AB .|. Ab).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are treated as invariable and necessary conditions of all thinking and logical symbols. They need not be specially laid down in proofs but are used explicitly in substitution methods and indirect inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Various forms of disjunctive propositions (single/double-sided, composites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disjunctive propositions occur in many forms: any number of alternatives; alternatives themselves may be combinations; propositions may be disjunctive in one or both members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of doubly disjunctive: 'Solids or liquids or gases are electrics or conductors of electricity' — meaning anything that falls under any left-side alternative must fall under one or more right-side alternatives. Complex definitions (e.g., Senior's definition of wealth) may be represented symbolically and developed into many alternatives; the form determines valid inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expand / develop composite alternatives to enumerated cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When a disjunctive term contains composed alternatives (e.g., BC(D .|. E)), expand it into all distinct enumerated alternatives (BCDE .|. BCDe .|. BCrfE, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developing alternatives clarifies the strict logical interpretation and allows explicit treatment of mutually compatible or incompatible subcases. The development shows how many specific cases arise (e.g., first alternative ABC can develop into eight cases depending on presence/absence of D,E,F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine a simple term with a disjunctive term by distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: To combine a simple term with a disjunctive term, combine it with every alternative: A(B .|. C) = AB .|. AC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'A vegetable is either a herb, a shrub, or a tree' therefore 'an exogenous vegetable is either an exogenous herb, or an exogenous shrub, or an exogenous tree.' This is the distributive rule for conjunction with disjunction and is essential for correct symbolic manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine two disjunctive terms by pairwise pairing of alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: To combine two disjunctive terms, form each alternative of one with each alternative of the other (like algebraic multiplication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: (A .|. B)(C .|. D .|. E) = AC .|. AD .|. AE .|. BC .|. BD .|. BE. Botanical example: flowering plants either exogens or endogens and either herbs, shrubs, or trees → six alternatives. This rule holds regardless of number of terms/alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference from denial of an alternative to affirmation of the remainder (requires incompatibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the denial of any one alternative, the affirmation of the remainder can be inferred only when the alternatives are inconsistent (exclusive) or when inconsistency is otherwise established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general result 'from the denial of any of the alternatives the affirmation of the remainder can be inferred' holds when the alternatives are intended to be exclusive; but many ordinary disjunctions are not inconsistent (e.g., 'gems are either rare stones or beautiful stones' does not imply a rare gem is not beautiful). The symbolic method gives only true conclusions; one must make explicit the tacit premise of inconsistency to derive modus ponendo tollens style inferences (example: salt vs fresh water requires asserting 'what is salt is not fresh').

rubrics_metrics.name: Unite the same qualifying term to each side of an identity (distribution over identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A qualifying adjective or term may be joined to each side of an identity, distributing across each alternative: from A = B .|. C infer AD = BD .|. CD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to produce further inferences (e.g., 'a gaseous element is hydrogen or oxygen or nitrogen or chlorine or fluorine' leads to 'a free gaseous element is free hydrogen or free oxygen...'; if one alternative is impossible under a qualification (e.g., colourless chlorine), that alternative disappears).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect Method of Inference (proof by exclusion / contraposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define or determine what a thing is by showing it cannot be anything else; use Laws of Duality and Contradiction via substitution to produce indirect proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method mirrors negative proofs in geometry (Euclid) and number theory (Erastosthenes' sieve). It is necessary for many truths that cannot be proved directly (e.g., primality, incommensurability). The method uses substitution together with Law of Duality (A = AB .|. Ab) and Law of Contradiction to derive contrapositive propositions and conclusions by exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Contrapositive Proposition in syllogistic inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain contrapositive forms (e.g., from Every not-B is not-A obtain Every A is B) and apply them by substitution to include moods of ancient syllogism (Camestres, Cesare, Baroko, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contrapositive is drawn via substitution. Examples: 'Whales are not true fish; true fish respire water' represented symbolically and transformed via contraposition. Baroko and other moods, difficult for old logicians, are handled naturally by indirect reduction through contrapositive substitution. The author cautions that the contrapositive must be properly formed using the laws of thought; tacit premises about inconsistency may be needed in some arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive of a simple identity and its consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: From a simple identity A = B one can derive corresponding negative identities (a = ab, b = ab) and then further equivalences (possibly a = b) by substitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: using Law of Duality derive negatives, substitute the identity for A or B into those negative forms, then combine to obtain further identities. Examples: from Mercury = liquid-metal infer Not-mercury = not liquid-metal; from A = B derive a = ab and b = ab and then a = b (showing corresponding negatives coincide). This is used to transform definitions into equivalent negative forms and to exclude items from classes.
